To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the typical feature in the diabetic rat is loss of metaphy-seal trabecular and periosteal expansion of the diapysis, and that these features may be important in the pathogenesis of diabetic osteopathy and the susceptibility to peri-articular fracture and Charot arthropathy.
type-2 diabetic rats show a decrease in vertebral body length, an increase in periarticular trabecular osteoporosis and periosteal expansion of long bone diaphyses.
diabetic osteopathy is characterized by a decrease in vertebral body height, a loss of trabeculae and an increase in periosteal circumference in the appendicular skeleton.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of an animal model for osteoporosis.
the development of a non-invasive method to study the pathogenesis of diabetic osteopathy.
the study of the skeletal changes in type-1 and type-2 diabetes and the mechanisms involved.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the typical feature in diabetic rats is loss of trabecalular bone and expansion (not thickening) of the diaphyses.
the diabetic rat model is a good model of human diabetic bone disease, and that the pQCT method is an excellent method to study bone in the diabetic rat.
the diabetic rat model is useful for studying the pathogenesis and pathophysiology of diabetes-related bone disease.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
diabetes is associated with an expansion of the cortical compartment of long bones and loss of trabeculae.
diabetic rats are characterized by expansion of the diaphragm and loss of trabeculae.
the diabetic rat is a useful model for studying diabetic osteopathy.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the risk of osteopathy in type-2 diabetes varies according to sub-region in a bone.
diabetic osteopenia is characterized by loss of trabeculae and expansion of the cortical bone.
the risk of fragility fracture in diabetes varies with bone sub-regions.
